tagline.text: A high peak in the Central Panay range, with a knife-edge ridge, mossy forest and seas of clouds

location.label: Location
location.text: Barbaza, Antique — trek starts from Lombuyan village (on the border with Jamindan, Capiz)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May dry season (river crossings risky in the rains)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱6,000–12,000 (per person, from Iloilo; varies with group size and schedule)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Iloilo International Airport (ILO) or Kalibo International Airport (KLO)

children.text: Mount Nangtud, at about 2,074 m, is the second-highest peak on Panay and one of the most demanding trekking objectives in the Philippines, climbed from Barbaza in Antique. It is an expedition-style trek of two nights or more through river trails, a knife-edge ridge and mossy forest.
Mount Nangtud is a high peak of the Central Panay Mountain Range, which runs north to south through the middle of Panay. Sources give its height as

. On Panay only Mount Madja-as to the northwest is higher, and in the Visayas as a whole it ranks third after Mount Kanlaon and Mount Madja-as. Officially it lies on the border between Jamindan in Capiz and Barbaza in Antique, and since the provincial boundary is said to be unclear, it is usually presented locally as a Barbaza mountain.

Difficulty is the main reason the mountain is famous. The mountaineering site Pinoy Mountaineer classes it as a major climb rated 8 out of 9 and says it cannot be done as a day hike. From the jump-off village of Lombuyan you walk about 6 hours up the Dalanas River, climb the Knife Edge and loose scree trails to the Rancho campsite at about 1,400 m, and then continue through mossy forest to the summit. The top is not a sharp point but a throne-like cluster of trees and moss.

The appeal of the mountain is that the scenery keeps changing. A tropical river gorge, grassy ridges with a knife edge that drops away on both sides, and mossy forest above 1,650 m follow one after another, and on a clear day you can see a sea of clouds and the folds of the Panay range. Fitness, gear, weather and a local guide all have to line up, so only a handful of groups climbed it each year, and you should not expect the facilities of an ordinary tourist site.

Some of the fee and timing information in this guide comes from 2015–2022 sources. Guide rates, permit costs, local security and entry conditions can change, so check the latest information with the Barbaza police station and a Lombuyan guide before you go.
The summit stands at about
, second only to Mount Madja-as on Panay. The two mountains are separated by the Dalanas and Kigas rivers, about
14 km
apart in a straight line. Seeing one from the other makes it meaningful for hikers dreaming of a Panay high-peak traverse.

This is the most photographed section of Nangtud. One side is a steep drop and the other a grassy slope, so wind and views are overwhelming as you walk. One trip report describes crossing it as dusk fell, so allow plenty of time to pass while there is daylight.
Most of the first day is spent following the river from the jump-off village. You climb gradually from near sea level to about
, crossing the river countless times, so sandals or water-friendly shoes work best. It is a good place to refill water, but the river rises quickly when it rains.

blocks.title: Mossy forest and sea of clouds

children.text: From about
above the Rancho campsite the forest is thickly covered in moss, and the summit is a cluster of mossy trees. The mountain is known for a sea of clouds on good days.

The route runs through a chain of campsites: Lombuyan, the camp at the end of the river, Pingan, Rancho and EBJ Peak. Pingan and Rancho usually mark the end of a day, and near Rancho is the last reliable water source on the mountain.

blocks.title: EBJ Peak and the summit section

children.text: From Rancho to the summit with light packs takes roughly
3–5 hours

one way, depending on the report. You pass EBJ Peak on the way. Exploration of the mountain is said to have begun in the 1970s through the efforts of Gov. Evelio B. Javier, who reportedly led an expedition himself (Wikipedia gives 1977), and EBJ Peak was named after the late governor by the Antique Mountaineering Society. Confirm the exact year locally.

In Lombuyan, guide families offer homestays with simple meal preparation and laundry service. There is no convenience store, only very basic sari-sari stores, so buy your food in Barbaza town beforehand.

items.title: Standard 3 nights 4 days
items.subtitle: Round trip from Lombuyan to the summit

children.text: Take a van leaving Iloilo's Molo Terminal at around

Ride a tricycle and a motorcycle taxi via Mablad (Kapuywan) to Lombuyan village. Settle plans at the guide's house and spend the night there, which makes the first day much easier.
Start around
and walk about
6 hours
up the Dalanas River, then camp at the end of the river or near Pingan. The loose scree trails and the Libtong River section are dangerous in rain.
Pass the Knife Edge and steep scree trails through Pingan and reach the Rancho campsite at about
. Depending on the report, you arrive late in the afternoon. Refill plenty of water at Rancho.
Leave before dawn with light packs and go through EBJ Peak and the mossy forest to the summit. After lunch at the top, return to Rancho and camp.
Start descending at dawn through Pingan, the river section, Lombuyan and Mablad back to Barbaza. The last vans to Iloilo leave early, so check times locally in advance.
These times are approximate, based on Pinoy Mountaineer (2015) and blog reports (2019, 2022). Your pace, the weather and river levels may add a day.
Leave Lombuyan at dawn and cover the river section and the Knife Edge in one day, reaching Pingan or Rancho. Walking time can exceed
12 hours
Go to the summit and back at dawn, then descend to Pingan. Depending on the report, Rancho to the summit takes about 3–5 hours one way, and the descent takes time too.
Leave at dawn, cross the river section, and move on to Lombuyan and Barbaza, report out at the police station and return to Iloilo.
The 2 nights 3 days plan means long walking days and a risk of crossing the Knife Edge after dark. Some reports mention passing the ridge in the dark, so it is better not to push too hard.

The dry season is the proper time for Nangtud. Pinoy Mountaineer calls it a seasonal hike and says the Dalanas River can be completely unpassable at the height of the rainy season.
March–May
is generally the safest, and in other months you should leave slack in the schedule for when the river is swollen.

One report also mentions descending by a back trail toward the Bulan-bulan campsite when the river was swollen. Right after rain, however, rivers change quickly, so follow your guide's judgment and check the latest forecast and river levels.

Before and after the climb you will stay in Iloilo City, Barbaza town, or a homestay at a guide's house in Lombuyan. A Lombuyan homestay was reported at about
a night in a single 2022 report (confirm locally), and the guide's family often prepares meals. For hotels in Iloilo, see the
Iloilo City
entry.

There are no restaurants on the mountain, so you must carry food for every day of the trek. Buy rice, canned goods, noodles, dried fruit and trail snacks at the Barbaza town market, and treat the sari-sari stores in Lombuyan as selling only the most basic items. Water is available at the campsites but you must purify it yourself, so bring purification tablets or a filter.
Register and obtain a permit at the Barbaza town police station before you set out. Some reports say a letter of intent is now required in advance, so get in touch before your trip.
Hire a guide in Lombuyan village. Reports mention local guide families, and you should not climb without a guide. Check recent reports for contact details.
You will cross rivers many times, so trekking sandals or quick-drying shoes are comfortable. Long pants are recommended to protect against cuts from cogon grass.
Leeches are common, so bring socks, gaiters and insect repellent.
The last reliable water source is near Rancho. There is almost none above it, so carry plenty of water for the summit push.
Mobile signal is almost nonexistent, so leave your itinerary with family and your guide and download offline maps.
If it rains, the decision to retreat from the river section is the most important one. Plan at least one spare day.
The summit section is slippery with moss and often foggy. A waterproof jacket and a headlamp are essential.

This is a major climb that cannot be done in a day; in the rains river crossings can block you in, and local security conditions have dampened hiking activity. Check the latest situation before you leave.
The Dalanas River is wide with many crossings and rises quickly in rain. If you cannot cross, turn back.
The Knife Edge has a drop on one side and strong wind. Manage your time so you do not walk it after dark or in fog.
The soil trail from the Libtong River to the Bulan-bulan campsite is loose, with a risk of slipping and falling rock.
Pinoy Mountaineer (2015) said that security concerns, including insurgency reports, have impeded hiking. Check the current situation with the Barbaza police station and the local government.
Some trip reports mention stomach pain and diarrhea, so always purify your water and bring basic medicine.
Fees and schedules in this guide mix 2015–2022 sources, so reconfirm the latest information locally.
A small island off Culasi in northern Antique, a good place to rest after the climb. Check locally how to get there from Barbaza and how long it takes.
The starting and ending base for the trek. You can catch the van to Barbaza at the Molo Terminal and add a day of city sightseeing.
The gateway city of Aklan, with Kalibo International Airport, convenient for combining with a Boracay trip.
Panay's highest peak, neighboring Nangtud. A traverse between the two has been reported but no established trail is known, so consult local guides.
